patient_counselling: Eye drop technique: wash hands; tilt head back; pull lower lid down to form a pocket; instill 1 drop into the pocket WITHOUT touching the dropper to the eye/lashes; close eye gently for 1–2 minutes, press finger over inner corner (punctal occlusion) to reduce systemic absorption and increase ocular contact; wipe excess.

If using ointment: pull lower lid down, squeeze a 0.5–1 cm ribbon into the pocket along the lower lid, close eye; vision will be blurry for 5–10 minutes after — apply at bedtime or when blurry vision is acceptable.
Wait at least 5 minutes between different eye drops if using more than one product. Apply ointments LAST.

For BACTERIAL conjunctivitis (purulent yellow/green discharge, eyelids stuck together in morning): use the prescribed antibiotic drop/ointment for 5–7 days; symptoms typically improve within 2–3 days.

For VIRAL conjunctivitis (watery discharge, often unilateral spread to other eye, frequent in adults): no antibiotic needed — self-limiting, resolves in 1–2 weeks; cool compresses and lubricating drops (preservative-free artificial tears) help symptoms.

For ALLERGIC conjunctivitis (bilateral itching, watery discharge, often with rhinitis): olopatadine (Pataday) once daily or ketotifen (Zaditor) twice daily; cool compresses, allergen avoidance, OTC antihistamine if associated rhinitis.

Hygiene: wash hands frequently; do NOT share towels, pillowcases, eye makeup, or contact lenses; discard makeup and contact lens cases used during infection; replace contact lenses; do not wear contact lenses until 24 hours after symptoms resolve.
Stay home from school/work until discharge resolves (typically 24 hours after starting antibiotics for bacterial; symptoms manageable for viral) per public health guidance.

Red flags — seek urgent eye care: vision changes/loss, severe eye pain, photophobia, corneal opacity, severe redness, contact lens wearer with red eye (risk of bacterial keratitis from Pseudomonas), neonates with eye discharge (gonococcal/chlamydial — emergency), trauma, foreign body sensation, herpes vesicles around eye (HSV keratitis).
Store eye drops at room temperature (or per label — some require refrigeration); discard 28 days after opening (preservative-containing) or per single-use vial directions; do not touch dropper tip.
therapeutic_flow: 1. Confirm Minor Ailments eligibility: Ontario resident with typical conjunctivitis presentation (red eye, discharge); verify ID/OHIP, obtain consent.

2. Focused history: discharge characterization (watery vs mucopurulent), unilateral vs bilateral, itch (favours allergic), associated URI or rhinitis, contact lens use, recent trauma, photophobia or vision changes, prior episodes, current medications.

3. Red flag screen: vision changes/loss, severe pain, photophobia, corneal opacity/ulcer, contact lens wearer with red eye, neonate with eye discharge (gonococcal/chlamydial — emergency), suspected HSV keratitis, foreign body, hyperacute purulent discharge (gonorrhea) — refer urgently.

4. Differential diagnosis: bacterial vs viral vs allergic conjunctivitis; rule out keratitis, uveitis, episcleritis, scleritis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, dry eye, blepharitis, subconjunctival hemorrhage.

5. Therapy selection: bacterial → tobramycin / fusidic acid / Polytrim drops × 5–7 days; viral → supportive (cool compress, artificial tears); allergic → olopatadine or ketotifen + allergen avoidance; reserve fluoroquinolones for contact lens wearers / suspected serious infection.
6. Counsel on eye drop technique (punctal occlusion, no contamination), hygiene, contact lens precautions, school/work exclusion, expected timeline, when to seek urgent care.
7. Document the encounter per OCP standards: assessment findings (type of conjunctivitis), diagnosis, therapy chosen, counselling provided, notify primary care provider.
8. Follow-up: reassess at 5–7 days for bacterial; if no improvement or vision changes, refer to ophthalmology; viral cases monitored for 1–2 weeks self-resolution.
